rows.rule: even n -> n/2; n=3 mod 28 -> n+28 (trap); other odd n -> n+7
rows.question: Which n have infinite orbits?
rows.answer: Exactly n = 3,5,6 mod 7 (the quadratic non-residues mod 7). n = 0 mod 7 ends in the cycle (7 14); n = 1,2,4 mod 7 ends in (1 8 4 2).
rows.method: Invariant: halving acts as x -> 4x on Z/7 and n+7, n+28 fix n mod 7, so A0={0}, A1={1,2,4}, A3={3,5,6} are each invariant. The n+7 map descends to [1,7], and a finite table gives exactly three cycles, one per class; the A3 cycle (3 10 5 12 6) contains the trap residue 3, so every A3 orbit is trapped and A0/A1 never are. Proof in census/round2/upfrom1/up_qr7.md, check in check_up_qr7.py (PASS).
rows.why_not_lower: Evidence only. The answer is a mod-7 condition, while the branches and the trap are 2-adic (mod 28); the trap has density 1/28 but the divergent set has density 3/7. The finite table cannot be dropped: moving the trap to 19 mod 28 (also in A3, also 3 mod 4) keeps the invariant but changes the answer, because 19 is not on a cycle (the check script tests this). So the answer depends on which residues lie on cycles.
rows.notes: I re-derived the proof: n/2 = 4n (mod 7) gives the invariant; the minimum of any g-cycle is <= 7, so the [1,14] cycle table is complete; the trap residue 3 lies on the A3 cycle. An independent memoized test of every n < 10^6 matches the mod-7 rule. Tier 2 because the proof needs a congruence invariant mod 7, which monotonicity and valuation arguments cannot see. The explorer's 'why not tier 1' is evidence, correctly labeled as such.

rows.rule: even n -> n/2; n=1 mod 4 -> n+3; n=3 mod 4 -> n+4 (trap)
rows.question: Which n have infinite orbits?
rows.answer: The orbit is finite (reaches 1->4->2->1) iff n = 2^a(4B+1) with B>=0 and every maximal 0-run of binary(B) of even length (trailing run included). Equivalently binary(n) is in (1(1|00)*01 | 1)0*. Every other n diverges. |E cap [1,2^k)| = F_{k+2}-1 (Fibonacci, checked k<=16).
rows.method: The orbit of 4B+1 reaches B+1. The recursion on B is: B odd gives Q(Y); B=4Z+2 is trapped; B=4Z gives Q(Z); B=0 gives 1. This is a 2-state LSB-first automaton with a reject sink, so the finite-orbit set is a regular language; the regex was checked against simulation for all n<2^16 and the rule for all n<2^18. General lemma: any trap plus n+d_r branches plus halving has bounded carry, so its answer set is always regular.
rows.why_not_lower: PROVED. A tier-2 answer is a finite union of residue classes changed on a finite set, so it is either finite or has positive density. E is infinite (it contains every 2^a) and has density 0, since |E cap [1,2^k)| <= sum F_{j+1} = O(phi^k). D has density 1 and an infinite complement. So neither E nor D has a congruence description.
rows.notes: The recursion, its termination and the regex are correct. The regex matches simulation for n < 2^21, and the count F_{k+2}-1 holds for k <= 21 (checked only, not proved). The proof that no congruence description exists is valid. Caveat: the method is an elementary mod-4 descent on B; tier 3 rests only on the answer being an automaton. The lens is inconsistent: under the ct* standard (answer = trap basin, decided in O(log n) steps) this system is tier 1. The general bounded-carry regularity lemma is sketched, not written out. The claimed exhaustive mod-8 search has no script.

rows.rule: n=3 mod 4 -> n+4 (trap); else even n -> n/2, odd n -> (3n+1)/2
rows.question: Which n have infinite orbits?
rows.answer: Exactly the n whose T-orbit meets 3 mod 4 before reaching 1. All other orbits reach (1 2); there is no other cycle and no untrapped divergence. Membership is decided in O(log n) steps.
rows.method: Two-step descent: off the trap, n=1 mod 4 maps to (3n+1)/2 and then (3n+1)/4 < n. Checked for n<300000. Not proved: whether the divergent set is a regular language. Nerode counts grow (1,2,4,6,8,11,16,23,33,48,70,101,146 for suffix lengths 0..12), which suggests it is not, so a closed description stays open.
rows.why_not_lower: Tier 1 is the floor for an infinite claim; simulation cannot prove it.
rows.notes: The two-step descent (3n+1)/4 < n is correct; the stopping-time tree closes at depth 2. Confirmed only as a GLOBAL claim (divergent set = trap basin). Under up_tok3's standard (closed description required) the question is OPEN, because non-regularity is only supported by Nerode counts. The question should be restated as GLOBAL.

rows.rule: n=7 mod 8 -> n+8; n=27 mod 32 -> n+32 (traps = parity words 111..., 11011); else even n -> n/2, odd n -> (3n+1)/2
rows.question: Which n have infinite orbits?
rows.answer: Exactly the n whose T-orbit meets 7 mod 8 or 27 mod 32 before reaching 1. Every other orbit reaches (1 2), with no other cycles and no untrapped divergence.
rows.method: A parity-word lemma plus a word lemma: 5-words avoiding 111 and 11011 have at most 3 ones. Then x_{t+5} <= (27x_t+58)/32, where b_max=58 is found exhaustively; this is below x_t for x_t>=12, and [1,11] is closed. A finite table over 1..11 finishes it, and every untrapped cycle meets [1,11]. The check covers all residues, the constants, and n<400000.
rows.why_not_lower: Partly proved: no window shorter than 5 contracts. Untrapped stretches with words 1, 11, 110 and 1101 exist (exhibited in the check), with multipliers 3/2, 9/4, 9/8 and 27/16, all >1, so one-step or short-block monotonicity fails. That no other tier-1 argument (such as a clever potential function) exists is only evidence.
rows.notes: I re-derived the word lemma, b_max = 58, the threshold 12, the cycle-minimum argument and the [1,11] table. A simpler stopping-time tree on residues mod 32 (stop words 0, 10, 1100, 11010) gives descent for all x >= 5 and shrinks the table to [1,4]. It is the same method as ct11 at depth 5, so the line between tier 1 and 2 here is size, not kind. The 'why not tier 1' only rules out uniform windows.

rows.rule: n mod 256 in R -> n+256 (R = 37 residues whose 8-step Collatz parity word has >=6 ones); else even n -> n/2, odd n -> (3n+1)/2
rows.question: Which n have infinite orbits?
rows.answer: Exactly the n whose T-orbit meets R mod 256 before reaching 1. All other orbits reach (1 2).
rows.method: Same scheme as up_ct35, with the window as close as practical to the critical density: untrapped 8-windows have <=5 ones (density 0.625 < log2/log3 = 0.6309). This gives x_{t+8} <= (243x+1688)/256, below x for x>=130, and [1,129] is closed. A finite table over 1..129 finishes it (checked for n<300000).
rows.why_not_lower: Evidence: untrapped stretches up to length 7 with multiplier >1 exist (e.g. 1101101, 3^5/2^7 = 1.90), so short-block monotonicity fails. The table size (129) and window (8) are forced by how close 3^5/2^8 is to 1.
rows.notes: |R| = 37, b_max = 1688, threshold 130 and the bound 129 all verified; the parity lemma holds mod 256. The stopping-time tree closes with maximal depth 8 and descent for x >= 25, so the table shrinks to [1,24]. Same tier. The 'why not lower' is evidence only.

rows.rule: n=7 mod 8 -> n+8 (trap); else even n -> n/2, odd n -> (3n+1)/2
rows.question: Which n have infinite orbits (is it exactly the trap basin, with (1 2) the only untrapped cycle)?
rows.answer: OPEN. The Collatz conjecture implies yes. Every n <= 2^68 is trapped or reaches 1 (Barina, J. Supercomputing 77 (2021) 2681-2688); the check verifies n<10^6.
rows.method: Tried the window-descent method of ct35/ct58. Proved it fails for every window length: 111-free words can have ones-density 2/3 > log2/log3, and for each j the residue class mod 2^{3j} with word (110)^j stays untrapped and multiplies by (9/8)^j. Congruence and automaton arguments also cannot exclude the pattern: (110)^inf is realized by the untrapped negative cycle -5 -> -7 -> -10. Known m-cycle bounds (Hercher 2023, m<=91) limit the number of odd runs, not their lengths, so they do not settle the cycle part.
rows.why_not_lower: Proved that the tier-2 method (uniform window descent plus finite table) cannot work, as shown above. That no other proof exists is only evidence: an untrapped divergent orbit would be a divergent Collatz orbit with every odd run of length <=2, and no known technique excludes one.
rows.notes: The computations, the (110)^j lift and the negative cycle -5 -> -7 -> -10 are verified. The Barina 2^68 bound (J. Supercomput. 77 (2021)) applies exactly; the Hercher m-cycle bound is correctly described. The stopping-time tree has 103 open branches at depth 30. I could not finish it. Caveat added: density above log2/log3 kills the descent method but does not by itself imply the system is open (counterexample in ct3.md, which is tier 1).

rows.rule: n even -> n/2; n odd -> (n+23c)/3, c in {0,1,2} minimal (c = n mod 3)
rows.question: BASIN: which cycle does each n reach?
rows.answer: If 23 | n, n reaches the fixed point 23. If the Legendre symbol (n/23) = +1, n reaches the cycle (1 8 4 2). If (n/23) = -1, n reaches the cycle (5 17 21 7 10).
rows.method: Lemma CD (coset descent): [1,q] is forward invariant, every n>q descends, and T(n) = m^{-1} n mod q, so gcd(n,q) and the coset of <2,3> are invariant. <2,3> has order 11, so it is the quadratic residues (2 and 3 are both squares since 23 = -1 mod 24). A finite table shows one cycle per class. Files: /home/riv/Code/collatz/census/round2/qr/qrA3_q23.md and check_qrA3_q23.py.
rows.why_not_lower: Evidence only. T is not injective on the box (T(2)=T(3)=1), so it is not conjugate to a rotation. Units with identical size and valuations (1 and 5) reach different cycles, so a congruence invariant is needed. We claim tier 2, not the rubric's tier 3 for 'QR invariants': the coset is read directly off n mod 23.
rows.notes: I re-derived Lemma CD: there is descent into [1,q], T(n) = m^{-1} n mod q, and the gcd and the coset are invariant. Part (c) holds because the rule is a class function. The check exits 0. My own test (step taken from systems.py, rule from Euler's criterion, no memoisation) gives 0 mismatches on [1,3e4] and on [1e12, 1e12+3000], and |H| = 11. The why-not-tier-1 argument is a sketch, not a proof, but it is acceptable. The proof is a congruence invariant plus an exhaustive table, which is tier 2.

rows.rule: n even -> n/2; n odd -> (n+307c)/3, c = (-n) mod 3
rows.question: BASIN
rows.answer: If 307 | n, n reaches 307. Otherwise the cubic character n^102 mod 307 decides: value 1 -> cycle through 1 (length 18); value chi(5) -> cycle through 5 (length 28); value chi(7) -> cycle through 7 (length 18).
rows.method: Lemma CD with H = <2,3> equal to the cubes mod 307. 2 is a cube because 307 = 8^2 + 27*3^2 (Gauss); 2^102 = 3^102 = 1 and |H| = 102 are checked. This is the first prime in the family where <2,3> has index 3 (searched q < 600). A finite table shows exactly one cycle per cubic class.
rows.why_not_lower: Evidence only. T is non-injective (T(2)=T(3)=1), and separating three cycles needs a character of order 3, which is a congruence invariant mod q. So tier 2.
rows.notes: Cycles through 1, 5 and 7 have lengths 18, 28 and 18, and {307} is a fixed point. I confirmed these independently. |<2,3>| = 102 = the group of cubes, checked by exact computation. The Gauss x^2+27y^2 criterion is cited correctly but is not needed. Independent rule test: 0 mismatches. Tier 2.

rows.rule: n even -> n/2; n odd -> (n+251c)/5, c in {0..4} minimal
rows.question: BASIN
rows.answer: If 251 | n, n reaches 251. Otherwise n reaches the cycle through r, where r in {1,3,7,9,21} is the unique element with r^50 = n^50 mod 251 (cycle lengths 8, 8, 15, 8, 8).
rows.method: Lemma CD with H = <2,5> = the fifth powers mod 251 (index 5; 2^50 = 5^50 = 1 and |H| = 50 are checked). A finite table gives one cycle per quintic class. For contrast, in the same family q=191 has 2 cycles per coset.
rows.why_not_lower: Evidence only. T(2)=T(5)=1, so T is non-injective. Separating five cycles needs an order-5 character, which is a congruence invariant mod q. So tier 2.
rows.notes: Five cycles with lengths 8, 8, 15, 8 and 8, plus {251}; confirmed. <2,5> = the fifth powers (order 50), checked. Independent rule test: 0 mismatches. Tier 2.

rows.rule: n even -> n/2; n=1 mod 4 -> (n+311c)/3; n=3 mod 4 -> (n+311c)/5; c minimal
rows.question: BASIN
rows.answer: If 311 | n, n reaches 311. If (n/311) = +1, n reaches the cycle through 3 (length 13). If (n/311) = -1, n reaches the cycle through 11 (length 16).
rows.method: Lemma CD, which allows any rule for choosing the multiplier. Here H = <2,3,5> = QR mod 311 by quadratic reciprocity, and |H| = 155 is checked. A finite table gives one cycle per class. The first index-3 (cubic) case for this map is q = 643.
rows.why_not_lower: Evidence only. T is non-injective on the box, and the cycles are separated only by a congruence character. So tier 2.
rows.notes: Descent holds for both branches: (n+2q)/3 < n and (n+4q)/5 < n exactly when n > q. |<2,3,5>| = 155 = QR. Cycles have minima 3 and 11 (lengths 13 and 16), plus {311}. Independent rule test: 0 mismatches. Tier 2.

rows.rule: n even -> n/2; n odd -> (n+95c)/3, c in {0,1,2} minimal
rows.question: BASIN
rows.answer: gcd(n,95) = 95 -> 95; gcd = 5 -> cycle (5 65 85 60 30 15); gcd = 19 -> cycle (19 38). For gcd = 1: Jacobi symbol (n/95) = +1 -> cycle (1 32 16 8 4 2); (n/95) = -1 -> cycle through 7 (length 12).
rows.method: Lemma CD for composite q = 5*19: gcd(n,q) and the coset in (Z/(q/d))^*/H are invariant. H = <2,3> has index 2 and lies in the kernel of the Jacobi symbol, since J(2) = J(3) = (-1)(-1) = 1, so H equals that kernel. Neither Legendre factor alone is invariant. A finite table gives 5 classes and 5 cycles.
rows.why_not_lower: Evidence only. T is non-injective on the box, and a congruence character mod 95 is required. So tier 2. Contrast q = 1081 = 23*47: 8 classes but 12 cycles, so the coset invariant fails there.
rows.notes: I re-derived the composite case. For d = 5 the class is a coset mod 19, and for d = 19 a coset mod 5. 2 is a primitive root mod both, so each of these is a single class. |<2,3> mod 95| = 36 = the Jacobi kernel. Cycles: 1 (length 6), 7 (length 12), 5 (length 6), 19 (length 2) and 95. Independent rule test: 0 mismatches. Tier 2.

rows.question: BASIN
rows.answer: 7 | n -> cycle (7 14). n a QR mod 7 -> cycle (1 18 9 22 11 16 8 4 2). n a non-residue mod 7 -> cycle (3 12 6) or (5 20 10): two cycles in one coset, decided by an explicit 20-state LSB-first binary automaton given in the md file. No rule of the form 'basin depends only on n mod M' exists for any M.
rows.method: Descent into [1,35]; T(n) = 4n mod 7 gives the coset invariant. A carry-transducer induction shows T^k(n) = 2*(n>>(k+1)) + b_k + s_k with bounded carry s_k. This yields a 38-state automaton, minimized to 20 states and verified against direct iteration for n < 2^18. Non-periodicity is proved: periodicity would force g(2x) = g(x), g(x) = g(x+35) and g(x) = g(x+21), hence g(x) = g(x+7), so the basin would depend only on the coset; but 3 and 5 share a coset and have different basins.
rows.why_not_lower: PROVED that tier 2 fails. The basin is not periodic for any modulus, so no congruence invariant, however fine, decides it, and coset plus finite table is insufficient. Tier 3 is reached by the explicit automaton certificate.
rows.notes: The carry induction is correct: c_r = r mod 2 makes the halving exact, and s stays <= 36. So the automaton is proved correct for all n; the comparison up to 2^18 is not what the proof rests on. I wrote my own carry recursion and checked it on 3000 random odd n of up to 400 bits: 0 mismatches. The non-periodicity proof is correct, and I strengthened it to rule out ultimate periodicity too (multiply by a large power of 2). That makes the why-not-tier-2 a real proof. Tier 3 is reached through the explicit 20-state DFA.

rows.rule: n even -> n/2; n odd -> (n+17c)/3, c = n mod 3
rows.question: BASIN (strong form): give a finite-state rule deciding whether n reaches (1 6 3) or (5 13 10), or prove none exists
rows.answer: Proved: the cycles are exactly (1 6 3), (5 13 10) and (17), all orbits reach them, and 17 | n iff n reaches 17. Also proved: no congruence rule separates (1 6 3) from (5 13 10), because the basin is not periodic mod any M; the coset invariant is trivial since <2,3> = (Z/17)^*. Open: whether any automaton in any base decides the basin. The base 2, 3 and 6 kernels grow without saturating (2^e, 3^e, and 1,6,29,65,140,329,856), which is evidence the basin is not automatic in those bases.
rows.method: Lemma CD gives descent and the cycle table. Non-periodicity follows from basin(2n) = basin(n) and basin(3n) = basin(n) for odd n: a CRT argument reduces any period to an m' coprime to 6, then g(x) = g(x+17) and g(3x) = g(x), and since 5 = 3^5 mod 17 this forces basin(5) = basin(1), a contradiction. Cobham's theorem then says the basin set is at most one of 2-automatic and 3-automatic.
rows.why_not_lower: PROVED that tier 2 fails (no congruence rule). The base-2 transducer method of qrB7_c53 breaks because division by 2 and by 3 mix the 2-adic and 3-adic digits, the Collatz-type obstruction. Non-automaticity is supported by evidence only. Tier 5 here is the nominal value for 'unresolved'; we do not believe the problem is Collatz-hard.
rows.notes: The proved parts are confirmed: cycles, descent, trivial coset, and the no-congruence theorem (5 = 3^5 mod 17). I strengthened the theorem to rule out ultimate periodicity, which Cobham's theorem needs. I also showed basin(3n) = basin(n) for all n, so the basin depends only on the part of n coprime to 6. Attempts to finish failed. Invariance under x2 and x3 does not force non-automaticity: {n : oddpart(n) = 1 or 3 mod 8} is 2-automatic, invariant under both, and not ultimately periodic. I found no periodic rule on n coprime to 102 for many moduli 17*2^a*3^b and 17*5*7*11*13 (n <= 2^21; tens of thousands of conflicts each). It remains OPEN. Tier 5 is nominal and does not mean Collatz-hard.

rows.rule: m=2 mod 3 -> (m+1)/3; else m odd -> (m+1)/2; else m even -> 3m/2. This is Farkas's F'(x) = x/3 if 3|x, (x+1)/2 if x=1 mod 4, (3x+1)/2 if x=3 mod 4, conjugated by x = 2m-1.
rows.question: GLOBAL: does every orbit reach the fixed point 1?
rows.answer: Yes. 1 is the only cycle. Correction to round 1: catalog farkas_s27 IS Farkas's map (YAH coordinates n=(x-1)/2): R(n) = G(n+1)-1 for n>=2, checked to 10^6.
rows.method: Strong induction. Even m=2^a c (m != 2 mod 3): a steps of 3m/2, one (m+1)/2 step, then a steps of (z+1)/3 along z_j=(3^j c+1)/2 = 2 mod 3. Lands at (c+1)/2 < m. Source: Farkas, Contemp. Math. 387 (2005) 121-127, Thm 1 (definition as transcribed in Yolcu-Aaronson-Heule arXiv:2105.14697, Sec. 4.2, Thm 4.2; Farkas's paper not read directly).
rows.why_not_lower: Tier 1 is the floor for a universal claim, since tier 0 cannot prove it. Note that YAH needed a 5x5 arctic matrix interpretation to prove it automatically, and default AProVE/Matchbox failed: a machine-hard but human-easy system.
rows.notes: I re-derived the conjugacy x=2m-1 and the block lemma; no gaps. The citation checks out against the YAH v3 text: Sec. 4.2 and Thm 4.2 'in the manner of Farkas [Far05, Theorem 1]'; default AProVE/Matchbox were 'too conservative'; the table lists Arctic dimension 5. Independently, every m<=3e5 reaches 1, and round-1 farkas_s27 equals YAH's F on [2,2e5), differing only at n=1, so the round-1 correction is right.

rows.rule: n=1 or 5 mod 8 -> 1; else even n -> n/2; odd n -> 3n+1
rows.question: GLOBAL: does every orbit reach 1? (= every Collatz trajectory meets 1 or 5 mod 8; YAH Sec. 4.5)
rows.answer: Yes. Every Collatz trajectory meets 1 or 5 mod 8 in finitely many steps.
rows.method: Case split mod 8. Odd 3 mod 8 goes to (3n+1)/2, which is 1 or 5 mod 8. Odd 7 mod 8 runs through 3^j 2^(a-j) b - 1 (valuation of n+1) until it reaches 3 mod 8. YAH state they proved it manually and automatically but print no proof.
rows.why_not_lower: Tier 1 is the floor. Notable: the tier-2 residue-graph-plus-potential method provably fails at every modulus 2^j, because class -1 carries the loop 7->6->7 of slope 3/2 (checked j<=64; max mean = log(3/2)/2 for j<=9). So valuation runs succeed where pure congruence certificates cannot.
rows.notes: I re-derived the proof: 3 mod 8 goes to 12q+5, which is in {1,5}; the 7-mod-8 valuation run ends at 4*3^(a-2)b-1, which is 3 mod 8. The YAH quote is verified ('proved both manually and automatically ... {1,5} and {1,7}'). The persistent -1 loop is a real proof that the plain graph method fails at every 2^j. Added: with the -1 node deleted, the max cycle mean is -log2, so 'accelerate -1 runs, then graph plus potential' is a complete method.

rows.rule: n=6 mod 8 -> 1; else even n -> n/2; odd n -> 3n+1
rows.question: GLOBAL: does every orbit enter {1,4,2}? (= YAH Prop. 4.7 / Thm 4.10, class 6)
rows.answer: Yes
rows.method: Odd iterates: class 7 is immediately forbidden. Class 1 gives (3n+1)/4, class 5 gives at most (3n+1)/8, and class 3 gives (3n+1)/2 but can only follow class 5. So the odd iterates not in class 3 strictly decrease, using the two-step bound (9o+11)/16 < o. YAH's own proof is the mod-8 residue graph (max mean log-slope -0.096) and needs a potential function to be rigorous.
rows.why_not_lower: Borderline 1/2: mod-8 transition bookkeeping plus one two-step descent inequality, with no table. I classify it tier 1, and a referee could reasonably say 2. Tier 0 cannot do universal claims.
rows.notes: I re-derived all mod-8 cases. The odd iterates in class 1 or 5 strictly decrease via (3o+1)/4 < o and (9o+11)/16 < o, with no threshold and no table, so this is tier 1, not tier 2. I checked YAH Prop 4.7 and Thm 4.10. Independent survey: every n<=3e5 enters {1,2,4}.

rows.rule: n=5 or 7 mod 8 -> 1; else even n -> n/2; odd n -> 3n+1
rows.question: GLOBAL: does every orbit enter {1,4,2}? (= Yolcu-Aaronson-Heule Conjecture 4.14, $500 prize)
rows.answer: Unknown. True for all n <= 10^6.
rows.method: Tried three approaches. (1) Residue graph plus potential: provably impossible at every modulus 2^j, because the 2-adic integer -7 has the C-cycle -7,-20,-10,-5,-14 (classes 1,4,6,3,2) of slope 9/8 (checked j<=64). (2) Valuation runs: each run of the reduced branch (9n+7)/8 is finite (8^r | n+7), but its interleaving with (3n+1)/4 (YAH Prop 4.15 map G) is a mixed expanding/contracting system. (3) No SAT tooling here (z3 not installed); YAH's matrix-interpretation search failed on it.
rows.why_not_lower: Proved: no tier-2 graph certificate at any 2-power modulus. Evidence only: the obstruction is the same interleaving structure as 3x+1, even though a G-step survives with 2-adic probability only 3/64.
rows.notes: This is exactly YAH Conj 4.14 ($500 reward for 4.11-4.14 verified), and the reduction to G matches YAH Prop 4.15; I re-checked it on lifts of all residues below 2^12. The -7 cycle of slope 9/8 is a valid all-j obstruction to the plain graph method. I could not finish the problem. Small error in the md: the open single classes are 0, 1, 5 and 7 per YAH; the md omits 7. Added a diagnostic (referee_avoid_graph_stats.py): the max mean cycle after deleting node -1 is negative for every solved set and positive for every open set at j=8.

rows.rule: even n -> n/2; odd n -> (3n+1)/2
rows.question: CYCLES restricted to 1-cycles (one maximal odd block then one even block): list them all
rows.answer: Only (1,2)
rows.method: 1-cycles with (k odd, l even) steps correspond exactly to d = 2^(k+l)-3^k > 0 with d | 2^l-1, which gives 0 < (k+l)log2 - k log3 < 2^(1-k). Rhin's bound |u1 log2+u2 log3| >= H^-13.3 (Rhin, Progr. Math. 71 (1987) 155-164, as quoted in Simons arXiv:2205.10582, Lemma 10) gives k <= 103. An exact scan of k <= 10^4 finds only (1,1). Original: Steiner, Proc. 7th Manitoba Conf. (1977) 553-559, via Baker. Caveat: Rhin's original not read, so its H-threshold is unverified; the scan covers H <= 2*10^4.
rows.why_not_lower: Evidence only: the obstruction is an exponentially good rational approximation to log2(3). Congruences cannot rule it out because, for each modulus, some residue pair (k,l) satisfies the divisibility. No elementary effective irrationality measure for log3/log2 is known.
rows.notes: I re-derived the cycle equation and its converse, l<=k, 0<Lambda<2^(1-k), the cutoff k<=103, and why only the least l can work. Rhin's bound holds for H>=2 per a secondary source (arXiv:2502.00948), so the explorer's caveat is resolved. Independent scan of k<=3000 over all l<=k+2 finds only (1,1). No lower-tier proof found: arXiv:1805.10496's algebraic proofs are conditional on an exponential bound on the iterates. why_not_lower is evidence, not a proof.

rows.question: CYCLES restricted to 1-cycles (one maximal block of non-multiples of 3): list them all
rows.method: A 1-cycle has minimum x0 = 2^l e and satisfies e(3^(k+l)-2^(2k+l)) = S with |S| <= 4^k-3^k. This gives k <= 2l+3, and for l>=2, |(2k+l)log2-(k+l)log3| < 2^(1-l). Rhin's bound then gives l <= 118. An exact scan of l <= 600 leaves five candidate (k,l) pairs; enumerating e for each finds the two cycles. This is an independent proof of the m=1 part of Simons arXiv:2205.10582 Cor. 11(a), without his X0 = 10^6 search.
